Erithacus rubecula.rmk: Although this clip of Robin song seems unexciting, it is anything but. The date was 24 June 2024 and the songster was a juvenile STILL IN COMPLETE JUVENILE PLUMAGE.  In fact, a second juvenile was in the same area and it can be heard singing (somewhat feebly) in the intervals.  Although very young (fledging date unknown) the two juveniles had already reverted to using song as a means of declaring and then defending territory. Free food (wax-worms) were available in the vicinity but the supply was cornered by one juvenile only. When the other appeared, it was singled out immediately for a 'missile' attack from the juvenile featured singing in the clip. The first sign of body moult - a red breast feather - did not appear until around the first day of July. For me, the use of song at such an early stage in the birds' 'adult-like' behaviour was surprising. I have heard juvenile Robin song before  - but only from individuals that had started to moult. This made me think that juveniles did not sing until they started to moult. An assumption proved wrong by this recording!

Erithacus rubecula.rmk:
This recording was made on Inishbofin, an island off the coast of Co. Galway where Robins are abundant. By the middle of August,  adults are in various stages of moult; some appear to be finished and the remainder are 'over the worst'. From around dawn, most adult Robins were singing - whether they were moulting or not.  Territories were being defended by these males - that must, in effect, be resident. The recording demonstrates two males counter-singing. Over the first 25 seconds, the two alternate song bursts, like tennis players.  However, after 0:25, one or both (sadly a plane passing overhead ruined a key part of the recording) switch to uttering a high-pitch 'siiiii' note. At the time, I could not hear the sound - hence I do not know if it came from just one or both. However, if you listen closely to the 'siiiii' notes at the 38th and 39th seconds, it sounds as if the two birds are using the  call in a kind of audio arm-wrestling. Examples of the high-pitched 'siiiiiii' are at 0:26, 0:29, 0:32; 0:36, 0:38 and 0:39. What happened next was fascinating - one flew straight on to a fence-post used by the other.  Its wing-beats can be heard at 0:40. The perched Robin flew off - without a fight. The trespasser uttered further 'siiiii' calls (now louder because it was closer to the recorder).  These are at 0:43, 0:45, 0:49 and 0:51. Having driven off the rival, the Robin then flew back from whence it came and resumed singing from within its own territory. You can hear if fly back close to the end of the clip at 0:52. 

Such behaviour is exciting to see in action. Use of the 'siiiiii' note in signalling aggressive intent could easily have been missed - because I could not hear the sound, except when the bird was within about 2m in the last ten seconds or so of the clip.

Erithacus rubecula.rmk:
I paid attention to this old and very bushy hedgerow as another observer had reported hearing Spotted Flycatcher song here. I could not find any flycatchers but I set up my recorder for a few minutes and it picked up these similar calls - in this case given by a Robin. From what I understand, these Robin"tsi" calls are higher pitched than Spotted Flycatchers' (6.0 - 8.8 kHz vs 4.8 - 7.6 kHz), have a single "kink" in the sonogram (SF often has spikes rising from an otherwise flat note) and are shorter (average of 89 ms vs 102 ms for SF). The notes here have lengths of 83, 94, 102 and 86 ms.
Unfortunately I did not see the bird giving the call. A number of recordings on XC attribute these "tsi" calls to juvenile Robins which may be the case here. 

Recorded with an Olympus LS-12 and Sennheiser ME66 placed on a tree branch. EQ adjusted below 1800 Hz to reduce distant road noise.

> when i was at this place at 22.07.17 morning... nearly the only birds i heard, were juv. Phylloscopus collybita with their adults - and there was strong calm of birds in the forest.

....>>> generally noted to moult: "The birds stop singing. Most birds already did, or sing infrequent. ---- Mating, nesting, breeding, feeding, caring. Exhausted. --- Renew worn plumage. --- Moult, fattening up for migration or the coming winter. ----- No need, no energy, no time to sing.

Robins occasional sing fast and intensely at a low volume. Other distinguishing characteristics of the practice include a lack of spacing between phrases. The function of the broadcast has been shoehorned under the heading 'subsong'. In THE BIRDS OF THE WESTERN PALEARCTIC (vol. 5) it states (pp 611): 'Subsong, given by both sexes in a variety of circumstances, is a subdued, complex and rambling warble containing discordant notes. Structurally more variable than full song and phrases not always apparent; when present, successive phrases often differ greatly in length (most 1 to 5 seconds). Mimicry more obvious than in full song.' I would agree with most of that. The attached clip was made in early spring (mid March) and two Robins were sitting relaxed within the bottom of a wide hawthorn hedge. The weather had been showery with rain squalls. The birds were probably taking the equivalent of a time out. I was within about three metres of them. One began singing and kept singing over about roughly 20 minutes (with occasional breaks).  Had I not been close, I would not have heard the sound at a range of, say, more than 20 metres. Was the songster a male serenading a female? I have no idea. Of course, the songster might even have been the female. On the clip, there is, to my mind, a striking piece of mimickry. In it the Robin goes from an imitation of a singing male Blackcap straight into notes of Great Tit (the fast, piston-like 'pink pink' that Great Tit seems to copy from Chaffinch). The Blackcap impersonation is at 0:13 (best in the fourteenth second); the Great Tit double note is at 0:15.
For more discussion about 'subsong' you may like to listen to another recording and read the accompanying comments at XC329370.

Este lugar es un rico mosaico de ecosistemas cuyo cordón umbilical es un cauce de arroyo ahora seco por la falta de lluvias que hemos tenido este otoño. Hay alguna alameda con árboles de sorprendente tamaño, carrizal y tarajal, pero la mayor parte de la vegetación de las orillas ha desaparecido por la acción de los agricultores. Más allá hay una serie de eriales, viñedos, cercados de ganado, pinares, y restos de bosques de quercíneas. Las grabaciones han sido realizadas en un pequeño cauce afluente del arroyo principal que debe tener un manantial por lo cual es el único lugar que ofrece agua disponible en una gran distancia. Por este motivo hay allí montones de pajarillos que por la tarde se congregan para bañarse y beber. Otro motivo es que la vegetación riparia formada por un denso zarzal y zonas de carrizo se ha respetado.

Esta zona boscosa es bastante peculiar por sus tintes atlánticos, ya que por su situación y altitud dispone de un clima relativamente fresco y húmedo. El sotobosque es muy rico e incluye helechos de buen tamaño, y las especies arbóreas son abundantes y destaca el variado elenco de quercíneas que hay en el lugar, en concreto cinco especies. Además este tipo de bosque se alterna con castañares y pequeños pueblos.

El hábitat es bastante peculiar con bosques en los que se encuentran varias especies de quercíneas alternados con cultivos de castaño. El sotobosque es muy variado y entre las especies con que cuenta están los helechos. Ello se debe a la altura de esta serranía, a la abundancia de cursos de agua y a la influencia atlántica del clima.

Song from a Robin in juvenile plumage. This youngster had scarcely moulted any of its juvenile body plumage. A few (whitish) adult-type lower belly feathers had grown through its juvenile underparts, as had a handful of orange feathers at the sides of the lower breast. The bird was tame and I had watched it infrequently over four days, during which time it only gave high-pitched siiih calls. On the morning when I was departing, I heard Robin song. I was astonished to see the juvenile singing, perched on overhead wires. I was not that close and rushed to make any kind of recording. I was just in time because a little over half-a-minute later, a door opened beside me which panicked two juvenile Backbirds 0:40 that flew and almost collided with the Robin. It flew too, ticking as it went 0:42. In the background, Hooded Crow just after 0:12 and a faint Meadow Pipit flying over at 0:29.

Turdus merula.rmk:
I heard this odd song alot this summer and at various times of day and also my neighbours heard it too. In the beginning I thought this was a car alarm and sometimes this sound could go on for so long. One day I spotted the bird sitting on top a rooftop and saw him singing on the same time as the sound and then I started hearing/seeing him everywhere around the house. I was very suprised by him making this type of sound since Ive never heard it sounding like it before.

The recording is not modified. Habitat is in the city between a house and a park in the recording. Ive often seen it sitting on top of rooftop singing but its usually on a little distance. Ive looked at it with  binoculars and pretty sure its a Turdus merula - black body with a orange beak.

Turdus merula.loc: Ireland (near  Bangor), Ards And North Down, Northern Ireland
Turdus merula.rmk: Blackbirds are renowned for being alarmists. This clip contains a selection of their edgy calls. Lower-pitched 'chook' calls feature at 0:01 (three repeats of the same note), 0:03 (two repeats) and 0:06 (three repeats). Two less loud 'chook' bursts follow. Higher-pitched 'chink' notes are at 0:09 (five repeats). Alarm rattles are at 0:11, 0:15, 0:20 and 0:25. After this, less loud 'chink' calls feature, giving way to a final 'chook' series (three repeats) at 0:27. Note how the three types of agitated calls - from lower chook to higher chink to 'wall of sound' alarm - are interchangeable and are at the whim of the bird. All calls were made by the same bird.

Turdus merula.loc: Ireland (near  Bangor), Ards And North Down, Northern Ireland
Turdus merula.rmk: A clip of Blackbird's assertive 'chinking' that is a common accompaniment to a lot of the bird's 'nosy parker' lifestyle and is especially used prior to roost. Two bursts of chinking are followed by the contact call from a juvenile (the high and rising whistle) and, finally, song from a nearby male. The recording was made in a garden where several Blackbirds commonly hung out.

Turdus merula.loc: El Baix Camp (near  Riudecols), Tarragona, Catalonia

Turdus merula.rmk: This clip is from a young male Blackbird, recorded on 19 September. The recording features what is loosely called 'sub-song'. I find that term ambiguous and unhelpful. The only vaguely apt part of the term is 'sub', implying that the 'song' is, in some way, inferior. Well, it may be inferior but it isn't really true song at all. Young Blackbirds and many other young songbirds need to develop singing skills and start the process during autumn and then winter. They are, therefore, practicing – and not singing properly. If they were singing properly, they would be doing so for one of two reasons: to proclaim ownership of territory or attract a mate. Not only are youngsters not bothering about either of these objectives, but their vocal performance, by its very nature, proves that they have a different purpose. In effect, they are practicing and singing to themselves. Rather than terming the sound 'sub-song', a better description might be 'self-song'. Three qualities show that the utterance is not meant for an audience. First, the vocals are very quiet and not audible except very close - within, say, five metres. This clip was recorded from a hidden microphone about 2m from the bird. Second, the vocalist is concealed, typically perched within a bush, hedge or thicket. Third, the composition sounds nothing like typical song and, in Blackbird, rambles on and on and contains interwoven notes that are part of the bird's full vocabulary. In this clip, although the voice is low and the components are not easy to distinguish, you can hear examples (rehearsals?) of the following: an alarm rattle at 0:01; juvenile screech-call at the end of 0:02 [a full recording from a juvenile is at XC180419]; two typical melodic song notes at 0:09; two nervous 'chook' calls at 0:20; a further alarm rattle – epitomising a flight alarm – at 0:21, repetition of song notes at 0:24 (a singing Blackbird quite often includes a few repetitions). The bird was well concealed in dense shrubbery throughout the recording. In total, it was 'singing' on and off for about twenty minutes. In the end it flew off silently. Hence, the flight alarms in the clip were actually given at rest. A gusty wind meant that large parts of the recording were inaudible. It is interesting that the weather - bad for birdsong - was no impediment. This is further support for the bird's vocalizing serving as a kind of private practice session.

Recorded:

  • alarm call, pli-pli-pli-pli-pli..., e.g. at 0:00.4 and 0:07.3

General observations: Mixed forest close to pasture lands. Blackbird calls from a grove of deciduous trees.

Other distinguishable species:

  • Mistle Thrush, Turdus viscivorus, alarm call, karrrrr, at e.g. 0:06.8
  • Willow Tit, Poecile montanus, call, (zi zi ) taah taah , at 0:05.6 (vaguely)
  • Great Tit, Parus major, call, che-che-che-che or chich-ich-ich-ich, at e.g. 0:14.4 (vaguely)
  • Eurasian Blue Tit, Cyanistes caeruleus, call, sisisi, at 0:21.6
  • Great Spotted Woodpecker Dendrocopos major, foraging, at e.g. 0:22.8

Sound classification and rendering: Svensson, Mullarney and Zetterström, 2009, Collins Bird Guide, Second Edition, HarperCollinsPublishers

Este lugar es un rico mosaico de ecosistemas cuyo cordón umbilical es un cauce de arroyo ahora seco por la falta de lluvias que hemos tenido este otoño. Hay alguna alameda con árboles de sorprendente tamaño, carrizal y tarajal, pero la mayor parte de la vegetación de las orillas ha desaparecido por la acción de los agricultores. Más allá hay una serie de eriales, viñedos, cercados de ganado, pinares, y restos de bosques de quercíneas. Las grabaciones han sido realizadas en un pequeño cauce afluente del arroyo principal que debe tener un manantial por lo cual es el único lugar que ofrece agua disponible en una gran distancia. Por este motivo hay allí montones de pajarillos que por la tarde se congregan para bañarse y beber. Otro motivo es que la vegetación riparia formada por un denso zarzal y zonas de carrizo se ha respetado.

Ambos lugares están bastante preparados, tienen observatorios para aves en las lagunas, puentes en los arroyos y caminos de tablas para un cómodo desplazamiento de los observadores. El ecosistema es bosque de pino y encina, en la Rocina predominan los primeros mientras que en el Alcebrón las segundas, alternados con lagunas y arroyos que se secan en verano y que están jalonados de vegetación palustre y de ribera tal como todo tipo de carrizos y juncos, árboles típicos de ribera, cañas y helechos. Lo cierto es que algo que llama la atención es que tanto en un bosque como en otro el arbolado está más enfermo de lo que debería, pues los pinos tienen mucho ramaje seco y se ven bastantes encinas muertas.

Since 12 February 2015 I have been hearing passages of Blackbird song in the latter part of the night. Sunrise is at around 0730hrs and singing starts roughly two hours earlier. Many Blackbirds are among local gardens (such as around 15 in my own garden measuring 15m by 10m) but the number singing is, at the moment (late February) very few. In the clip, just a few verses are delivered (five in 26 seconds). The gaps are long. Indeed, other unused parts of the same performance had even longer gaps. However, the phrases, when compared with a male (XC180806, also at dawn) in the breeding season are less energetic and attenuated. To my ear, a Blackbird in 'full voice' generates emphasis from each completed phrase. I can equate the bird's 'rising strangle' to wringing moisture from a towel.  Moreover, there is almost a tummy-tightening sensation in the intonation. But not so much in this bird's efforts. Possibly it is a young male; possibly it is too early in the season for it to really get going? On the subject of Blackbird song in late winter it is worth repeating the discoveries of D.W.Snow, as described in his book, A Study of Blackbirds. ' The first song of the year is nearly always heard in the late afternoon, often at dusk; dawn song begins a few days later. Gradually the afternoon period extends back into the earlier part of the day, so that after two or three weeks song may be heard at any time. For the first six weeks of the song period, until about the end of March, nearly all day-time song is from young males. Old males sing sporadically at dawn, and on fine evenings at dusk, but hardly at all in the middle of the day. I noticed this early in 1953, and thereafter systematically noted the age of males singing in the early part of the season. From February to mid-March I was able to distinguish the age of 62 singing males, of which all but seven (89%) were first-year birds.'

Turdus merula.rmk: The recording documents a typical winter sound made by Blackbirds that accumulate in my garden thanks to regular feeding (of dry porridge oats). Over several years this scenario has occurred: autumn migrants visit and new birds join others until as many as 15 are present and feeding on a lawn measuring just under 10m in length and 8m in width. In fact, many more than 15 Blackbirds are involved and the turnover reflects fresh winter influxes. The majority of both sexes are first-winters. Nonetheless, a basic 'pack mentality' develops and trees and hedges bordering the lawn act as safe gathering areas prior to feeding. When several Blackbirds are in the vicinity and at least one is feeding (the first to feed appears always to be silent), others are tempted to drop onto the lawn or sneak onto it from hiding places under hedges. When a few are gathered, the low parping starts. Irrespective of whether there is a handful of Blackbirds (such as 3 or 4) or up to 12, the incidence of calling seems fixed at about the same output. The sound's function might be to appease neighbours and permit several birds to feed in fairly close company and with a reasonable amount of harmony (although disputes are also common). Another possibility is that the calls themselves, if overheard by other Blackbirds, denote a feeding opportunity. Perhaps the calls serve as a kind of 'excuse me, would you mind if I joined in?' Hence the calls are given both by birds on the ground and from others that are perched or otherwise hidden but that are clearly interested in the feeding activity. Each seems independently minded but, in the quest for food, pragmatism brings several into closer-than-normal company. Somehow, the calls have a role in the behaviour. In my opinion, the calls are non-aggressive and also have no alarm value.

Turdus merula.rmk: Male Blackbird perched in a Birch tree. Given the date, it was completely dark and the bird may have been disturbed from its overnight roost in a nearby conifer hedge. The Birch is partly illuminated by street light and often holds a winter-singing Robin (that was also present and can be heard in the background). The Blackbird called repeatedly for about one minute. It then flew off. Shrill call from a juvenile well hidden in vegetation. According to Birds of the Western Palearctic and Snow (1958) - A Study of Blackbirds - the shrill contact call develops as the fledged juvenile becomes progressively independent of its parent.  Like the staccato call (XC 180418) the shrill call is designed to be uttered by a 'parked' youngster waiting to be fed.

Staccato calls from a juvenile Blackbird. According to Birds of the Western Palearctic and Snow (1958) - A Study of Blackbirds - the sharp and very loud calls are used by hidden fledged young when out of the nest but with only limited powers of flight.
